episode_title: Buying a Dental Practice: What Are You Actually Paying For?

real_qa.q: What financial metrics should a dental practice buyer analyze beyond the asking price when evaluating practice value?
real_qa.r: When purchasing a dental practice, you must understand the quality, sustainability, and transferability of cash flow and goodwill. A buyer should analyze collections rather than production alone, review two to three years of financials to identify trends, examine normalized expenses, evaluate hygiene production metrics, assess accounts receivable handling, and determine what the practice will realistically earn as owner after debt service. Revenue and EBITDA by themselves do not tell the full story.
real_qa.requete: how to value dental practice buying acquisition

real_qa.q: Why is the difference between production and collections critical when buying a dental practice?
real_qa.r: A practice might produce $1.5 million but only collect $1.2 million, which is a very different economic picture. You need to understand gross production, adjustments, write-offs, net production, and collections, then ask what contractual adjustments exist, what is being written off, what the collection percentage is, and whether there is significant old accounts receivable. A buyer should never evaluate a practice based on production alone; collections is the actual number that matters.
real_qa.requete: production vs collections dental practice valuation

real_qa.q: What is debt service coverage ratio and what minimum threshold do banks typically require for dental practice acquisitions?
real_qa.r: Debt service coverage (DSC) is calculated as revenue minus operating expenses minus reasonable doctor compensation, divided by debt obligations. Banks typically do not want a one-to-one ratio where one dollar in equals one dollar out. Most banks look for something greater, typically 1.2 or 1.25, meaning for every dollar that goes out, banks want $1.20 to $1.25 coming in. This is the average minimum debt service coverage ratio banks will accept.
real_qa.requete: dental practice debt service coverage ratio bank requirements

real_qa.q: What three numbers must a dental practice buyer clearly understand before determining if a purchase price makes sense?
real_qa.r: Before moving forward in any acquisition, a buyer must be able to clearly articulate three numbers: first, what does this practice collect; second, what does this practice actually earn after normalized expenses; and third, what will the buyer realistically earn as the owner after paying debt and operating expenses. If you cannot answer those three questions clearly, you are not ready to determine whether the purchase price makes sense.
real_qa.requete: three numbers dental practice buyer should know acquisition

real_qa.q: How should a dental practice buyer evaluate the impact of seller dependency and clinical production when assessing practice value?
real_qa.r: A buyer needs to determine what percentage of the practice's profitability is actually compensation for the doctor doing the dentistry. Two practices collecting identical revenue may have very different values depending on how much the seller produces clinically. If the seller is producing a huge percentage of revenue, transition risk may be higher. The buyer should calculate profit after paying reasonable clinical compensation for the dentistry performed, which is a much better way to assess sustainable economics and reduce risk.
real_qa.requete: seller clinical production dependency dental practice value

real_quote: Revenue does not determine the value of a dental practice. Collections do not determine the value. You're buying future cash flow.
